newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICO DEBT OUTLOOK-Mexico to offer new Euro issue.
newsitem.headline: MEXICO DEBT OUTLOOK-Mexico to offer new Euro issue.

text.p: Mexico is on the verge of tapping capital markets with an 11-year 750 million mark issue on the back of the continuing upbeat sentiment for Latin American debt, analysts said.
The latest Eurobond from the United Mexican States (UMS), Mexico's formal name, is seen coming out this week.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell confirmed on Tuesday from London it had been chosen as lead manager for the issue.
"My sense is that the reception that Latin America has been getting has been quite robust," said Bankers Trust economist Carl W. Ross. "The environment has been favourable."
If the past two mark-denominated bond issues are anything to go by, the size of Mexico's latest planned mark issue could also be bumped up.
Mexico last placed a bond in marks in February, issuing a 12-year 1.5 billion mark placement at 264 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. That issue was originally planned to be only 1.0 billion marks.

The issue before that, an eight-year placement in September 1996, was also originally planned at 1.0 billion marks but was also bumped up to 1.5 billion marks. It was placed at 304 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Mexico has been extremely active in the last month in capital markets with investors shrugging off the upcoming mid-term elections on July 6 that had been expected to cause more market turmoil.
"In general, people have been sanguine about the election cycle," said Ross.

For example, Mexico was able to announce in mid-June it would call $6.0 billion in five-year floating rate notes that had been backed by Mexico's oil revenues. That placement had originally helped Mexico pay back some of what it owed to the U.S. government as part of the emergency aid package.
The Finance Ministry said it would finance that deal with debt launched earlier this year and with some fresh deals.
Among the moves it made was to expand its 10-year global bond issued in January to $1.5 billion from $1.0 billion and to announce $1.0 billion in five-year floating rate notes.
After that the Mexico also issued a seven-year 500 billion lira bond and said it would also use these funds for the August 6 amortization of the floating rate notes.

Those moves, and the planned mark issue, fit in with Mexico's strategy of extending the maturities of its debt. Analysts say Mexico is leading Latin American nations in stretching out its yield curve.
Moreover, demand for Mexican paper remains unabated.
Santander Investment noted recently that the floating rate note deal "sends a positive signal that international markets are hungry for Mexican risk given the promising economic perspectives."
"The placing of the (mark) bond... could give a boost to the markets, showing more than anything the interest that there is abroad for Mexican debt," said one dealer on Mexico's stock market.
